title: Pocket Harvest: Inference Notes & Skims
content:
Quick context:
- Fast skims from NeurIPS workshop + a few arXiv posts. Mostly thinking about what impacts Redwood runtime: KV cache layout, batching heuristics for heterogeneous GPUs, low-bit quant stability, and cheap regression checks for quality after quant/merge.
- Format: one-paragraph summary, why it matters (prod), quick idea, and a 1-line experiment plan.

Papers / posts I skimmed:
1) Sparse-attention for long contexts (arXiv 2602.01234)
- TL;DR: cheap block-sparse attention that patches standard transformers with local + stride-based global windows; claims near-linear memory for very long sequences while keeping perplexity drop <2% on long-text LMs.
- Why it matters for Redwood: Could reduce KV cache memory pressure for long-session apps (chatbots, logs ingestion). Might enable higher effective context with same GPU RAM.
- Idea: implement a compatibility shim that converts model attention patterns at runtime (fallback to dense for small sequences).
- Quick experiment: run pretrained 7B on 16k inputs with block-sparse kernels vs baseline; measure per-token latency change and perplexity on our internal eval prompts.

2) Low-bit quant drift & recalibration note (community post)
- TL;DR: straight 4-bit post-training quantization causes subtle bias drift in logits when prompts include rare tokens; small calibration (per-layer bias correction + second-order scaling) recovers most of the gap.
- Prod impact: customers use quantized variants for Dedicated/Dedicated Private to cut cost; we need fast, robust calibration in the compile pipeline.
- Idea: integrate a lightweight bias histogram collector during warmup traffic to auto-apply a per-layer offset before enabling quantized model in live traffic.
- Experiment: simulate warmup of 1000 real queries, compute bias corrections, deploy to canary. Measure delta in top-1 and calibration.

3) KV-shard placement for multi-GPU streaming (workshop talk + slides)
- TL;DR: Sharding KV cache across GPUs by temporal locality (recent tokens colocated with compute) reduces cross-GPU transfers but requires dynamic remapping for rollouts.
- Why Redwood care: our batching/streaming runtime currently partitions by tensor parallel dims or simple round-robin. Temporal colocating could reduce NVLink traffic for long-session low-latency flows.
- Risk: remapping on long-lived sessions introduces map-update overheads and race conditions.
- Experiment idea: emulated shard placement with our runtime (small scale): compare NVLink bandwidth and per-token latency for 8k context with naive vs temporal shard mapping. Add a fallback that migrates lazily.

4) Lightweight end-to-end eval hooks (paper + open-source harness)
- TL;DR: tiny eval suites (5–10 synthetic prompts per feature) that are cheap to run on warmup traffic to detect semantic regressions after quant/opt. Use rank-based metrics + QA style checks.
- Product alignment: ties directly into Redwood Optimize and rollout automation: canary gating should include a small quality check, not just perf/latency.
- Quick plan: create a repo 'infer-eval-hooks' with 8 starter probes for generation (toxicity/faithfulness / repetition), and wire it into canary pipeline.

Notes / immediate thoughts:
- Mixing these approaches: temporal KV sharding + block-sparse attention may conflict because sparse kernels assume contiguous memory layouts. Need to prototype both together to catch fragmentation costs early.
- Calibration warmup: for Dedicated and Private, warmup traffic might not exist. Add synthetic warmup generator (from customer-provided examples) as part of deploy recipe.
- Operational affordance: expose a toggle in Console per-deployment: "enable fast-quant-calibration" that shows last-calibration timestamp and drift score.

Open questions / unknowns:
- How much extra JIT/compile time for block-sparse kernels on our current kernel-selection graph? Is this acceptable for hosted rapid model uploads?
- What are memory fragmentation patterns when we combine KV-shard remapping + batching across many small requests?
- Are there failure modes where calibration overfits warmup data and increases hallucinations? Need safeties.

Action items (next week):
- [ ] Prototype block-sparse kernel shim on 7B model (Owen assigned?) — measure compile time and peak memory.
- [ ] Build tiny canary eval suite (3 probes) and wire to rollout A/B in Console (I'll stub in repo).
- [ ] Run emulated KV-shard placement in local cluster; collect NVLink metrics.
- [ ] Draft short runbook for "quant calibration" including synthetic warmup recipe and rollback heuristics.

Quick links & references:
- arXiv (sparse-attention): https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01234
- KV-shard talk slides (NeurIPS workshop): https://neuralips-2026.org/schedule/workshop/inference-scaling
- Internal PR for KV experiments: https://github.com/redwood-inference/kv-shard-experiments/pull/42

Random scribbles:
- If we can get a safe default "calibrate on first 5000 tokens, then freeze" we can show 95% of customers immediate win without extra UX friction.
- Consider an API flag: prefer-latency vs prefer-cost, which picks shard/quant/attention tradeoffs automatically.

Thoughts for long-term research linkback:
- Add a small section in the model onboarding checklist for "attention locality profile" (histogram of attention span) so model catalog can suggest sparse/dense variants.
- Track a metric: "KV fragmentation ratio" (fragments / total KV bytes) and plot over time per-deployment. Might be helpful for SRE when diagnosing GC-like pauses.

End of notes. Short, messy — meant to capture ideas while fresh.
